_about: Every recommendation BodySync makes should point to an entry here. 'status' says how well it is backed: verified (primary source read in a search), secondary (reported by an article), unverified (no source found yet; do not present as fact).

entries.claim: Resting longer than about 60 seconds between sets gave a small muscle-growth benefit, and no clear difference showed beyond 90 seconds.
entries.evidence: systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis (2024)
used_in: rest timer: 90 s for lighter weighted lifts, 60 s for bodyweight

entries.claim: Resting 3 to 5 minutes between sets produced greater absolute strength gains than 1 minute.
entries.evidence: review of rest intervals in strength training (2009)
used_in: rest timer: 2.5 minutes for heavy barbell compound lifts

entries.claim: Missing one day often leads people to quit; streaks that reset daily can cause anxiety. Weekly goals, grace and lifetime totals are suggested alternatives.
entries.evidence: design articles citing habit research (Lally); not a fitness-specific study
used_in: Home flames count the current week; lifetime totals never reset; welcome-back messages

entries.claim: Core stabilisation exercises were no more effective than other active exercise for long-term back pain.
entries.evidence: systematic review with meta-analysis, 29 trials (BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2014)
used_in: wording of core and abs routines

entries.claim: Add 2-10% load once you can do 1-2 reps over your target on two sessions in a row (smaller increases for small-muscle exercises).
entries.evidence: ACSM position stand, Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults (2009); evidence category B
used_in: Add weight suggestions on the session screen: two sessions at the top of the range (or one that felt easy)
weight jump: the usual step, or half of it for light weights so it stays near 10%
entries.action: When you beat your rep target by 1 or 2 reps two sessions in a row, add a little weight. BodySync suggests it for you.

entries.claim: Gentle movement on a rest day counts as rest.
entries.evidence: no source found; this is a low-risk suggestion, not a recovery claim
used_in: Home rest-day block

entries.claim: For flexibility, ACSM suggests holding each static stretch about 10 to 30 seconds (30 to 60 seconds may help older adults more), on at least 2 to 3 days a week; daily works best.
entries.evidence: ACSM stretching and flexibility guidelines update (2021)
used_in: flexibility skill drills and holds (splits, touch your toes)
entries.action: Hold each stretch 10 to 30 seconds (30 to 60 if you're older), on at least 2 or 3 days a week.

entries.claim: Total stretching time per week mattered more than time per session; range of motion improved when stretching added up to at least about 5 minutes a week per muscle group.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis (2018)
used_in: flexibility skills: practise several times a week
entries.action: Give each area at least 5 minutes of stretching a week in total, for example 2 holds of 30 seconds on 5 days.

entries.claim: For people new to lifting, ACSM's position stand suggests total-body sessions 2 to 3 days a week.
entries.evidence: ACSM position stand, Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults (2009): novices train the entire body 2-3 days a week (primary text read)
used_in: curated full-body workouts for beginners
Home: repeat the starter or last curated workout 2-3 times a week
Plan my week: the suggested week is whole-body sessions on the goal days, a day apart
entries.action: Do 2 or 3 full-body sessions a week, with a day off between them.

entries.claim: Training each muscle about twice a week gave more muscle growth than once a week in a meta-analysis; when total weekly sets were equal the difference was small, so total sets matter most.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis (2016), with later volume-equated analyses
used_in: curated upper/lower and full-body workouts: repeat each about twice a week
Plan my week: with 4+ days and 3+ tracked lifts, upper and lower alternate so each is trained twice
entries.action: Train each muscle on 2 days a week, splitting the same total sets across them.

entries.claim: Adding reps at the same weight and adding weight at the same reps gave similar muscle and strength gains over 8 weeks.
entries.evidence: randomised trial, 43 trained adults, 8 weeks (Plotkin et al., PeerJ 2022)
used_in: 'Same weight, aim for one more rep' suggestions
bodyweight lifts progress by reps, then a harder version

entries.claim: 150 to 250 minutes a week of moderate activity mainly prevents weight gain and gives modest loss; more than 250 minutes a week is linked to clinically significant loss, and activity works best alongside a moderate diet.
entries.evidence: ACSM position stand, Appropriate physical activity intervention strategies for weight loss (Donnelly et al. 2009); abstract read
used_in: Plan my week, goal Lose weight: walks on the non-strength days, with the minutes explained
entries.action: Build up to more than 250 minutes of walking a week (about 35 minutes a day), alongside eating a little less.

entries.claim: Adding resistance or aerobic exercise to a calorie deficit helps lose fat while keeping lean mass.
entries.evidence: network meta-analysis of 62 randomised trials, 4,429 people (Frontiers in Nutrition 2025)
used_in: Plan my week, goal Lose weight: strength training stays in the week
entries.action: Keep at least 2 strength days a week while you lose weight, so what you lose is fat, not muscle.

entries.claim: Adults should do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week (or 75 to 150 vigorous), plus muscle-strengthening activity.
entries.evidence: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (executive summary)
used_in: Plan my week, goal Stay healthy: two strength days plus walks
entries.action: Walk briskly 30 minutes on 5 days (150 minutes) and do strength work on 2 days.

entries.claim: In one small lab study (16 people, a single session), the 12-3-30 incline walk burned calories more slowly than running but used a higher share of fat. It has not been tested for weight loss.
entries.evidence: exploratory study, International Journal of Exercise Science 2025
used_in: walk option 'Incline walk (12-3-30)', shown with this caveat

entries.claim: More weekly sets per muscle gave more muscle growth, with diminishing returns at higher volumes.
entries.evidence: meta-regression, 15 studies (Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger 2017)
used_in: Plan my week, goal Build muscle: more training days when you have them, each muscle twice a week
entries.action: Work up to about 10 hard sets per muscle each week, for example 3 to 4 sets for that muscle on each of 2 or 3 days.

entries.claim: Training only the lowering phase and training only the lifting phase gave similar gains in lifting strength, and lowering-only training built more lowering strength. The studies used lab machines, not push-ups or pull-ups.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis of eccentric-only vs concentric-only training (2025)
used_in: skill steps: slow-lowering versions count as another way to clear a step

entries.claim: Knee and toe push-ups worked the same muscles in similar proportions; toe push-ups worked them harder overall.
entries.evidence: EMG study of 12 men (Journal of Applied Biomechanics), as reported by Les Mills
used_in: push-up ladder: easier variations count as ways to clear a step

entries.claim: Short static stretches (60 seconds or less per muscle) had only a trivial effect on strength and power, while longer holds caused clear drops. Moving (dynamic) warm-ups are preferred right before training.
entries.evidence: review of acute static stretching effects (Chaabene, Behm and colleagues, 2019)
used_in: warm-up: moving exercises, no long holds, before strength work

entries.claim: A warm-up with lighter sets of the same exercise helped maximal strength and reps in several studies, though results were mixed.
entries.evidence: systematic review of 11 studies (Ribeiro et al., Motricidade 2021)
used_in: warm-up tip: one or two light sets of your first lift

entries.claim: An active cool-down did little for soreness or next-day performance in most studies; it may help heart rate and breathing settle sooner.
entries.evidence: narrative review (Van Hooren and Peake, Sports Medicine 2018)
used_in: cool-down: optional, described honestly; its stretching time counts toward flexibility

entries.claim: Six weeks of ab exercises alone (7 moves, 5 days a week) did not reduce belly fat or waist size, though ab endurance improved.
entries.evidence: randomized controlled trial, 24 adults (2011); a 2015 trial in women dieting found the same
used_in: Flat stomach program: walking + strength, core for strength not fat loss

entries.claim: More daily steps meant lower risk of early death, leveling off around 6,000-8,000 steps a day for adults 60 and over and 8,000-10,000 for younger adults.
entries.evidence: meta-analysis of 15 cohorts, 47,471 adults (Lancet Public Health, 2022)
used_in: daily step goal in the weight-loss and walking programs
entries.action: Build toward 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day (6,000 to 8,000 if you're 60 or over).

entries.claim: Protein helped strength training build muscle, with no further gain in muscle above about 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-regression, 49 trials, 1,863 people (Br J Sports Med, 2018)
used_in: Nutrition: daily protein target

entries.claim: Aim for about 0.4 g of protein per kg of body weight per meal, over at least 4 meals, to reach 1.6 g per kg a day.
entries.evidence: narrative review (J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2018)
used_in: Nutrition: protein per meal

entries.claim: New habits took 66 days on average to become automatic (18 to 254), and missing one day did not undo progress; only very irregular people failed to build the habit.
entries.evidence: real-world habit study, 96 people (Eur J Soc Psychol, 2010)
used_in: programs: show up 3 days a week, any days

entries.claim: Exercise therapy reduced knee pain and improved function for people with knee osteoarthritis.
entries.evidence: Cochrane review, 44 trials (2015; updated 2024)
used_in: Strong knees program

entries.claim: Pilates probably eased chronic low back pain more than minimal care, but not more than other exercise.
entries.evidence: Cochrane review, 10 trials, low to moderate quality (2015)
used_in: Pilates-style mat core

entries.claim: Training one body part did not reduce the fat over it: a meta-analysis of 13 studies (1,158 people aged 14 to 71) found no spot reduction (pooled effect -0.03, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.05).
entries.evidence: systematic review with meta-analysis, 13 controlled studies (Ramirez-Campillo, Human Movement, 2021)
entries.action: To lose fat in one place, lose fat overall: move more each day and eat a little less. Training the area builds the muscle underneath.
used_in: For your goal notes (abs, arms, glutes)

entries.claim: In a review of 67 EMG studies (1,247 adults), free-weight lifts such as squats and deadlifts drew the most activity from the six-pack muscle, the outer obliques and the lower back; core-stability moves such as planks drew the most from the inner obliques. The deepest layer (transverse abdominis) has been little studied.
entries.evidence: systematic review of electromyography studies (Oliva-Lozano and Muyor, IJERPH, 2020); measures muscle activity, not growth
entries.action: Keep squats, lunges and deadlifts in your week: they work your core too, alongside planks and dead bugs.
used_in: For your goal notes (abs, core)
move_targets.json: plank, side bridge, squats

entries.claim: Light and heavy weights grew muscle by a similar amount when sets were taken close to failure; heavy weights gave more gain in maximal strength.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis, 21 studies of at least 6 weeks (Schoenfeld, J Strength Cond Res, 2017)
entries.action: For firmer, more defined muscle, any weight works if the last 2 or 3 reps of each set are hard. For the most strength, go heavier.
used_in: For your goal notes (arms, glutes, muscle, strength)

entries.claim: Overhead cable triceps extensions grew the triceps about 1.4 times more than arms-down extensions over 12 weeks (whole triceps +19.9% vs +13.9%), even with lighter loads.
entries.evidence: within-person trial, 21 untrained adults, MRI (Maeo, Eur J Sport Sci, 2023); cable only
entries.action: Include one triceps move with your arms overhead, such as the seated triceps press.
used_in: move_targets.json: Seated Triceps Press
For your goal note (arms)

entries.claim: Hip thrusts and back squats grew the glutes by a similar amount over 9 weeks; squats also grew the thighs more. The hip thrust's higher muscle activity did not predict more glute growth.
entries.evidence: randomized trial, 34 untrained adults, MRI (Plotkin, Frontiers in Physiology, 2023)
entries.action: Bridges, hip thrusts, squats and lunges all build glutes. Pick the ones you enjoy and add weight or reps over time.
used_in: For your goal note (glutes)
move_targets.json: hip thrust, bridges

entries.claim: Strength training through a full range of motion improved flexibility as much as stretching, in 11 trials (452 people); the studies differed a lot in design.
entries.evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis of supervised randomized trials (Afonso, Healthcare, 2021)
entries.action: Lift through the full, comfortable range (deep squats, long lunges, full Romanian deadlifts): it counts toward flexibility too.
used_in: For your goal note (hips)

entries.claim: Early strength gains come largely from the nervous system learning the move, while muscle growth also starts from the beginning of training.
entries.evidence: narrative review (Folland and Williams, Sports Medicine, 2007)
entries.action: Expect to get stronger in the first weeks, before you see any change.
used_in: For your goal notes: when to expect change
Feeling stuck? on Progress

entries.claim: Muscle size was measurable on scans after 3 weeks of hard training (thigh +3.5 to 5.2%) and +6.5 to 7.4% after 5 weeks: real changes, but small.
entries.evidence: training study, 7 young adults, flywheel leg extensions (Seynnes, J Appl Physiol, 2007)
entries.action: Give a plan 9 to 12 weeks before judging it in the mirror; the growth studies BodySync uses ran that long.
used_in: For your goal notes: when to expect change
Feeling stuck? on Progress

entries.claim: Several nights of short sleep in a row reduced strength on multi-joint lifts such as squats, but not on single-joint moves; one night without sleep had little effect.
entries.evidence: systematic review, 17 studies rated moderate or weak quality (Knowles, J Sci Med Sport, 2018)
entries.action: If your big lifts have stalled, look at your last few nights: several short nights in a row lowered strength on lifts like squats.
used_in: Feeling stuck? on Progress
